Normalization and the new extremal consequenceThe normalization proof remains valid with the now-explicit assumptions that the graph is finite and simple,  $M$  is a matching, and  $T\cap V(M)=\varnothing$ .For a bundle promoting  $X$  and deleting its mates  $Y$ , with  $|X|=|Y|=k$ ,
$$T'=T\cup X,\qquad
P'=P\setminus(X\cup Y),\qquad
A'=A\setminus Y.$$
Therefore
$$|T'|+|M'|=(|T|+k)+(|M|-k)=|T|+|M|.$$
A nonempty bundle strictly decreases  $|M|$ , so at most the original  $|M|$  bundle steps occur. Matching replacement can include retaining the current matching.Component factorization also remains correct. A promoted endpoint has no endpoint neighbors in another component of  $G[P]$ ; deletions in another component therefore cannot make an otherwise impossible local promotion feasible. Current selections remain occupied, while their occupied neighborhoods can only shrink. This justifies both restriction of a bundle to one component and extension of a local step by unchanged data elsewhere.The single-terminality conclusion follows: an endpoint of occupied degree at most two can be promoted after deleting its mate.The extremal argument is validOn a fixed finite graph, there are finitely many feasible pairs. Choose a pair lexicographically maximizing
$$\bigl(|T|+|M|,\ |T|\bigr).$$
Any matching replacement followed by a nonempty feasible bundle would preserve the first coordinate and strictly increase the second. This contradicts the choice of the pair. Hence such an extremizer is exchange-terminal.The counterexample version is equally valid. On a fixed board, let
$$\mathcal C=\{(T,M)\text{ feasible}: |T|+|M|>mn/2\}.$$
If  $\mathcal C\ne\varnothing$ , choose a member maximizing  $|T|$ . An exchange followed by a nonempty bundle preserves the objective, so the resulting pair remains in  $\mathcal C$ , while its selected count increases. Again this is impossible.Thus a valid exchange-enabled local configuration can be excluded from these extremal representatives. This argument does not require a U/rotor source decomposition.The fixed-board qualification matters only to avoid taking a maximum over boards of unbounded size. Nothing in the proof requires such a global maximum: one counterexample board would suffice for the argument.2. The matching-independent motif and its algorithmThe completion condition is sufficientLet  $Q$  denote the six displayed old edges, and let  $S=V(Q)$ . Those six edges are disjoint and cover all twelve vertices of  $S$ .If
$$S\subseteq P
\quad\text{and}\quad
G[P\setminus S]\text{ has a perfect matching }C,$$
then
$$M^*=Q\cup C$$
is a perfect matching of  $G[P]$ .This construction does not depend on how the current matching meets  $S$ . In particular, current matching edges crossing between  $S$  and  $P\setminus S$  cause no difficulty: the matching is replaced globally by  $M^*$ .Because replacement preserves  $T,P,A$ , it preserves feasibility. The square exchange and five-edge promotion then apply exactly as in §3.Accordingly, an exchange-terminal pair cannot contain the specified endpoint/blank pattern together with the perfectly matchable-complement condition. That qualification is part of the forbidden configuration. The proof does not show that the endpoint and blank labels alone are forbidden.Completion is a substantive conditionThe four-vertex-path example is correct. A path on four vertices has a perfect matching, but its middle edge cannot belong to a perfect matching.The same distinction can occur for the actual twelve-site motif, so the issue is not merely an unrelated general warning. For example, let
$$u=(5,5),\quad v=(5,6),\quad
a=(5,4),\quad b=(4,6),$$
and take
$$P=S\cup\{a,b\},\qquad T=\varnothing,$$
with all other sites blank. Replace the edge  $uv$  in  $Q$  by the two edges
$$ua,\qquad vb,$$
retaining the other five edges of  $Q$ . This gives a perfect matching of all fourteen endpoints and preserves the three required blanks.However,
$$P\setminus S=\{a,b\},
\qquad \|a-b\|_1=3,$$
so  $G[P\setminus S]$  has no perfect matching.Thus occupancy of  $S$ , the three blank sites, and existence of a current perfect matching do not automatically permit installation of the six prescribed local edges. This example establishes that the completion hypothesis is substantive for the stated matching-extension argument. It is not a claim that a configuration failing this condition cannot admit some other promotion.The motif-specific procedure is polynomialThe algorithmic claim is justified by more than termination alone:A fixed twelve-site motif has only linearly many anchored placements and eight orientations.Each label check has constant size.Each complement-completion test is a polynomial bipartite matching problem.Each accepted motif step removes five matching edges.A full scan is repeated until none succeeds.For a concrete conservative bound, let  $N$  be the number of vertices of the explicit input grid. Its number of edges is  $O(N)$ . An elementary augmenting-path implementation can find a maximum bipartite matching in  $O(N^2)$  time: there are  $O(N)$  augmentations, each found by an  $O(N)$  graph search.Therefore:One completion test costs  $O(N^2)$ .One scan of  $O(N)$  placements costs  $O(N^3)$ .There are  $O(N)$  successful steps, followed by a final unsuccessful scan.This gives an  $O(N^4)$  upper bound without requiring a sharper matching algorithm. $$\left\lfloor\frac{|M_0|}{5}\right\rfloor.$$
If ordinary single-edge promotions are interleaved, the total number of successful steps is at most  $|M_0|$ .The search must be repeated after changes, including optional promotions: new blank sites and changed completion possibilities can enable a motif that previously failed.
